nodes.title: Root cause: expose({start(){}}) methods not extracted - shorthand methods in object literals missing from analyzer
Which object literal patterns to support
All three: exported objects, non-exported assigned objects, objects as function arguments
Only assigned objects (export const api = {}, const utils = {})
Only exported objects (export const api = {})
Naming scheme for object literal methods
Use :: consistently: file.ts::api::method for assigned, file.ts::expose(0)::start for arguments
Use dot notation: file.ts::api.method (like class methods)
All function forms are equivalent: function X, const x = function, const x = () =>, { method(){} }, { method: () => } - only 'this' binding differs (not tracked by mycelium)
For anonymous objects as arguments: use functionName(argIndex) as synthetic variable name, e.g. expose(0)::start for first arg's start method
For anonymous objects: include LOC to differentiate multiple calls. Format: file.ts::LOC:funcName(argIdx)::method e.g. file.ts::10:expose(0)::start
Final naming scheme for anonymous object args: file.ts::scope::[line:col]funcName(argIdx)::method - brackets clearly mark call-site location, separates from :: hierarchy
Example: curry({ a(){} }).next({ b(){} }) at line 20 becomes file.ts::[20:0]curry(0)::a and file.ts::[20:18]next(0)::b

Louvain algorithm (graphology-communities-louvain)
Infomap algorithm (@mapequation/infomap)
Leiden algorithm (improved Louvain)
Label Propagation Algorithm
Louvain: O(n log n), modularity-optimization, graphology-communities-louvain on npm, works for directed graphs. Resolution parameter controls community size. May produce disconnected communities.
Infomap: O(m log n), uses random walks and information theory, @mapequation/infomap npm (WASM). Best for directed graphs - detects flow-based communities. Hierarchical output.
Leiden: Fixes Louvain's badly-connected community problem. Guarantees communities are internally connected. No mature JS impl - would need WASM port or use Python subprocess.

For call graphs: Infomap is theoretically best (models information flow), Louvain most practical (pure JS). 2025 research: Leiden+Louvain most effective overall. Recommend: Start with Louvain (easy), upgrade to Infomap for production.

KEY INSIGHT: Let analysis branch out, don't try to capture conditionality.

The rule:
1. CAN trace method (user code) → follow actual dataflow inside
2. CAN'T trace method (built-ins like .map/.filter, externals) → branch with "may depend" edge

- CAN trace, so follow the actual parameter → usage → return flow
- Get precise edges, not approximations

nodes.title: Scopes = JS scopes exactly: module, function, block. Binding belongs to one scope. Reference crossing = side-effect. Severity = boundaries crossed.
Composition: scopes as components with ports. Captures = input ports (from parent). Yields = output ports (to parent). Each scope only tracks own bindings. Cross-scope via port edges.
Separate data-flow (values through bindings) from control-flow (how execution exits). Scopes have multiple exit points: return, break, yield, throw. Each exit has associated data-flow.
Use case unclear. Complete control-flow capture impossible in dynamic JS. Value is in net of relations + scope boundary crossings - reveals codebase structure that reading cannot.
Mycelium as topology analyzer, not semantic analyzer
Focus on scope boundaries and crossing patterns rather than execution semantics
Two layers: 1) Static topology (scopes/crossings) 2) Data-flow within scope (input→output chains). Can 'execute' dataflow to get transitive dependencies of outputs.
Branches: capture all paths, don't resolve which. Output depends on union of all possible paths. Conservative/sound - shows everything that COULD affect output.

Intent-first programming: code should be a derivative of intent, not a separate artifact requiring constant interpretation. Current LLM workflows are noisy because they reverse-engineer intent from code.

GAN metaphor for human-AI collaboration: humans specify structure/blocks (macro), AI fills in detail (micro). Like sketching composition and having model paint texture. Token-based LLM interface is wrong abstraction layer.

WASM/WAT as compilation target: minimal syntax (S-expressions = trees), type-safe, portable (browser/server/edge), AI-friendly. Graph nodes → WAT functions/structs, edges → references/calls. Human rarely touches WAT directly.

Bidirectional mapping is critical: changes to intent graph update code, changes to code update intent graph. Without bidirectionality, architectural drift still happens - AI paints on top of mistakes.

Static analysis + constraint validation underutilized in LLM workflows. AI could drive CLI tools to: cluster similar constraints, highlight conflicts, track invariants against code, enforce conventions. Type-checking for intent, not just syntax.

Mycelium as foundation for intent-first programming: already tracks semantic structure (scopes, crossings, data-flow). Missing pieces: constraint encoding, simulation layer, bidirectional sync with source, LLM-driven synthesis from graph.

Layered architecture vision: Human Intent (words/constraints) → Shared Intent Graph (nodes/edges) → AI Synthesis + Static Analysis → Code/Artifacts. Feedback loops close the gap: simulation → graph → human refinement.

Deciduous captures decisions, mycelium captures code topology. Together they could form the 'shared intent substrate' - deciduous tracks why (reasoning/goals), mycelium tracks what (semantic structure).
Restructure repo as monorepo with v0 as first exploration
v0 = TypeScript static analysis → queryable graph. Good foundation but analyzes existing code. Future versions could explore intent → graph → code (the inverse direction from ChatGPT conversation).
Restructured repo as monorepo with packages/v0 containing TypeScript analyzer
Monorepo structure in place: packages/v0 contains TypeScript analyzer, root ready for future packages
Created VISION.md documenting intent-first programming vision
VISION.md committed - captures layered architecture, bidirectionality requirement, deciduous+mycelium integration, and what's missing to reach the vision
Diffusion models for code: iterative refinement (propose → critique → refine → converge) instead of single-shot generation. Maps well to architecture evolution.
Editable latent spaces: edit intent directly without patching artifacts. Today's LLMs only let you edit output (code), not the latent intent that produced it. The graph IS the editable latent space.

Neuro-symbolic systems: symbolic (graphs, constraints, types) + neural (fuzzy generative detail) share state. Symbolic = discrete logic. Neural = fills in texture. Together = intent ↔ implementation bridge.

Differentiable programming/compilers: gradient-based optimization over implementation space. Declare constraints ('minimize latency under budget X'), compiler searches for optimal implementation. Tools: JAX, Halide, TVM/MLIR.
World-model AIs: persistent understanding of states, goals, actions, consequences. Avoids stateless LLM drift. The graph serves as the world model - persists across sessions.
Tool-using agents: LLM invokes solvers, CLI, compilers, simulators, verifiers. Offloads precise work to deterministic tools. LLMs reason; tools verify. Division of labor is key.
LLMs are stochastic approximators, not solvers. Good for fuzzy reasoning and synthesis. Constraint enforcement needs deterministic tools (SAT/SMT solvers, type checkers, simulators).

Dual-mode representation: Words (flexible, intuitive, ambiguous) + Graphs (precise, machine-readable, explodes in complexity). Words drive graph creation; graph operations feed back to narrative. Need both, bridged together.

Messy graph is a UX problem, not inherent. Mitigations: hierarchical abstraction (subgraphs), semantic folding (show relevant nodes only), temporal layers (old decisions fade), hybrid views (macro vs micro), AI-driven cleanup.

Words as soft constraint language: treat narrative as declarative layer encoding goals, constraints, invariants, assumptions. AI interprets and proposes graph structure. User speaks intent; AI populates graph. Human-AI co-authoring.

Maintenance burden killed by automation: two-way sync (edit words → graph updates, edit graph → words summarize), change tracking/diffing, auto-pruning/clustering, simulation/live feedback. Human resolves conflicts, not redraws everything.
v1: Graph ↔ WAT + Simple Constraints - prove graph is primary, code is derived, constraints validated deterministically
v1 scope: graph schema, graph→WAT generation, WAT→graph parsing, constraint validation CLI. No LLM, no UI, no simulation.
Scaffolded v1 package: graph schema, WAT generation/parsing stubs, constraint validation

Recursive box model (Russian doll): same structure at every zoom level. Node has ports, children, edges, constraints. Leaf = function, node with children = module. Graph = root node. No separate 'kinds' needed.
Implemented recursive box model: Node with ports, children, edges, constraints. WAT gen/parse updated. Constraint validation recursive.

Graph embeddings: project nodes into n-dimensional vector space based on structure, ports, constraints, neighborhood. Similar components cluster. Enables pattern detection, anti-pattern detection, abstraction candidates, semantic search.
Embedding space IS the editable latent space from neuro-symbolic vision. Symbolic graph + neural embeddings. Diffusion models could work in this space. AI-driven cleanup via clustering.

Prior art: Neuro-symbolic program synthesis - combines neural nets + symbolic reasoning. Programs invoke neural nets as library routines. GNNs for program analysis. Key refs: UT Austin neurosymbolic programming, SIGPLAN blog.

Prior art: Dataflow/visual programming - LabVIEW (1986), Node-RED, Pure Data. Block diagrams with wires. Execution when inputs available. Inherently parallel. Software engineering motivation, not just parallelism.
Prior art: Model-Driven Architecture (OMG) - Platform-independent models → code. Executable UML/fUML. Transformations: PIM → PSM → code. Forward engineering from models.

Prior art: Unison language - code identified by hash of AST, not names. Immutable definitions. Eliminates builds and dependency conflicts. Names are pointers to hashes. Distributed programming simplified.

Prior art: Synchronous reactive languages - Lustre, Esterel, Signal. Dataflow for reactive systems. Formal semantics enable verification. Used in safety-critical embedded (aerospace, automotive). SCADE industrial tool based on Lustre.
Prior art: Simulink/SCADE - industrial block diagram tools. Block diagrams → C/C++/CUDA/Verilog. Production-quality embedded code. Simulation before commitment. Hierarchical abstraction.
Prior art: Intentional Programming (Simonyi, Microsoft 1991-2001) - programs stored as intention trees, not text. Domain experts describe behavior, system generates code. Acquired by Microsoft 2017.

Prior art: JetBrains MPS - projectional editor, no parsing. AST is the source. Supports tables, diagrams, math notation mixed with text. No ambiguity when composing languages. YouTrack, mbeddr built with it.

Prior art: Bidirectional transformations / Lenses (Boomerang, UPenn) - programs that work forwards AND backwards. Get/put semantics. Used in parsers/printers, constraint maintainers, schema evolution. Key for graph ↔ code.

Prior art: Sketch (Solar-Lezama, MIT) - programmer writes partial program with holes, synthesizer fills them via constraint solving. CEGIS: counterexample-guided inductive synthesis. Scaled to real programs (AES cipher).
Prior art: Alloy (Jackson, MIT) - lightweight formal methods. Declarative specs in relational logic. Automatic analysis via SAT solving. Small scope hypothesis: most bugs found with few objects.
Prior art: TLA+ (Lamport) - formal specification for concurrent/distributed systems. Model checking finds bugs. Used at AWS, Microsoft. Exhaustively-testable pseudocode, blueprints for software.
Prior art: Racket / Language-Oriented Programming - solve problems by making DSLs. Macros as compiler extension. Any syntax maps to AST. Beautiful Racket book. Datalog, Algol60 as libraries.
Prior art: Eve (Chris Granger) - relational/Datalog core, literate programming environment. 30+ iterations. Temporal logic + relational datastore. Shut down 2018 but ideas live on.
Prior art: Dark (Paul Biggar) - deployless, holistic language+editor+infrastructure. Structured editor prevents invalid syntax. 50ms deploys. Language, editor, infra as one thing.
Prior art: Hazel - live functional programming with typed holes. Incomplete programs typecheck and run. Holes track closures. Integrates LLM synthesis. Distinguished papers at POPL, OOPSLA.
Prior art: Subtext (Jonathan Edwards) - program representation IS execution. Like spreadsheet, always live. Edits are semantic transformations. Copy-based programming model.

Why Intentional Programming didn't ship: (1) Microsoft prioritized C#/.NET over IP in 2001, (2) Intentional Software never finished product in 10+ years, (3) adoption barrier - must rewrite legacy + change skills, (4) intent→code transformation hard to get reliable, (5) ideas not novel enough to justify switch.

Lessons from IP failure for mycelium: (1) need forcing function for adoption (LLMs?), (2) must ship incrementally - 10yr without product = death, (3) graph→code must be reliable, (4) consider interop with existing code vs requiring rewrite.
Mycelium is NOT a new language. Graph is the abstraction layer; output is existing languages (WAT, TS, Rust). Don't repeat Intentional Programming's adoption barrier mistake.
Graph is queryable database, not drawable canvas. Programmer queries ('what calls X?', 'show dataflow'), system generates view. No manual node arrangement. Views are projections, not source.

Whiteboard metaphor: annotation layer floats on top of auto-generated visualization. Human can select nodes, add comments, draw. Annotations don't fight layout - they anchor to nodes or become orphaned if structure changes.
Time travel via git + deciduous: 'show me the graph at decision #42'. Git commits snapshot state, deciduous nodes capture reasoning, conversations link to both. Full provenance chain.

UI flow: conversation + canvas side by side. Chat for intent/discussion with LLM. Canvas for visualization/annotation. Comments on canvas link to chat messages. Chat links to timeline (git, deciduous).

The loop: (1) converse - describe intent, (2) synthesize - LLM adds constraints to graph, (3) visualize - explore macro/micro/dataflow, (4) annotate - draw on canvas, (5) persist - chat→deciduous, state→git, (6) time travel, (7) iterate.
Everything links to everything: canvas annotation → chat message → deciduous observation → git commit → graph state. Full bidirectional provenance. No orphaned context.
Roundtrip problem: Graph → WAT → Graph'. If user edits WAT, how to update graph? Metadata (edges, constraints) shouldn't clutter WAT output. User shouldn't maintain metadata manually.

Code edits as annotations: user editing WAT is like annotating on the whiteboard. System must infer intent from diff. Risk of misinterpretation - decoding intent from code is exactly what we're trying to avoid.
Options for WAT editing: (A) WAT read-only - all changes via graph, (B) diff and infer - risky, (C) suggestions - user confirms proposed graph changes, (D) separate patch layer - like git rebase.

Deeper question: is WAT the artifact users should edit? Maybe graph = macro (structure), WAT = micro (implementation). User edits WAT for micro details, graph for macro. Mismatches flagged, not auto-resolved.
Roundtrip strategy: code edits trigger intent derivation process
Code must be readable AND editable - essential to mycelium's goal, not optional. Read-only WAT is off the table.
Intent derivation as collaborative process: code edits WILL break graph in various ways, reconciliation happens through human-AI conversation to synthesize intent from diff
Two edit modes: (1) Annotations - added directly to intent graph, explicit mapping (2) Code edits - intent inferred through human-AI mediation. Annotations are easy path, edits are hard path.
Annotations are multi-surface: (1) on graph directly, (2) in chat with LOC links, (3) in code via comments. All feed same intent graph. Chat links need content-hashing for time-travel validity.
v2+ scope: implementation of hashed links, stale link handling, multi-surface annotation sync. Conceptual model settled, defer implementation.
v1 scope reduction: graph→WAT only, defer WAT→graph parsing to v2+

Mycelium is the gradient from vision to AST - one graph, multiple resolutions. Not separate intent vs implementation graphs, but zoom levels in a unified structure. Edges connect across abstraction levels.
Introspection like git blame but for intent: any LOC traces back through graph layers to its origin in vision/goals. Full provenance chain from implementation to intent.
Reverse introspection: start from goal, see all code that implements it. 'Show me everything that exists because of this decision.' Impact analysis for intent.
Cross-layer edges needed: 'implements', 'achieves', 'derives_from' relations that connect abstraction levels. Not just horizontal edges within a layer.
v0 traces implementation-level (call graphs, dependencies). Missing piece: upward links to intent. v1+ could prototype explicit 'implements' edges from concrete to abstract.
v2 direction: full gradient experiment with simple use case (calculator)

v2 calculator example spanning full gradient: Vision ('reusable math') → Architecture ('calculator system') → Components ('arithmetic ops') → Functions ('add', 'subtract') → Dataflow (a + b) → AST (i32.add). One use case, all layers, cross-layer edges.

C4 is descriptive (diagrams for humans), mycelium must be functional (layers that participate in generation/validation). If a layer doesn't compute anything, it's just documentation cruft. Layers must earn their existence.

Middle layers (architecture, component) earn their place through coordination, not compilation: AI↔human, human↔team, human↔self. Queryable, traceable, communicable - they're the 'why' that introspection reveals.

Prior art: MLIR - multiple abstraction levels in ONE IR via dialects, progressive lowering from high-level to machine code. Each level enables different optimizations. Key: levels aren't separate, they're dialects that get lowered.

Prior art: Nanopass - compiler as many small passes, each does ONE thing with explicit input/output language. Languages defined by diffs. Output verified well-formed. Key: small transformations, not monolithic layers.

Prior art: Refinement/Liquid Types - types + logical predicates ({x: Int | x > 0}), specs embedded in code, verified at compile time via SMT. Key: specs and implementation live together, not separate documents.

Applying prior art to mycelium: MLIR dialects → layers as dialects in unified graph. Nanopass transforms → small verified passes between layers. Refinement types → constraints as part of nodes, validated. All computational, not documentary.

Mycelium is a compiler of intent. Traditional compiler: source → IR → machine code. Mycelium: intent → architecture → components → functions → dataflow → AST. Input is intent, output is executable code, process is progressive lowering with verification.
Verification approach: Simulation/behavioral equivalence - run both levels with same inputs, compare outputs. Higher level as spec/mock, lower level as implementation. Like SPICE simulation in EE.

Verification approach: LVS-style structural comparison - extract structure from lower level, compare to higher level. Finds shorts, opens, missing components. 'Not only manufacturable, but represents what you intended.'

Verification approach: Property-based testing (QuickCheck) - define properties that should hold, generate random inputs, check. If counterexample found, shrink to minimal failing case. Fuzzing for correctness.
Verification approach: Translation validation (CompCert) - don't prove compiler correct in general, verify each specific lowering preserved semantics. Cheaper than full formal verification.
EE parallel for mycelium verification: Schematic→Intent layer, Layout→AST layer, Simulation→run both levels compare, LVS→structural match check, DRC→constraint validation.
Mocking as verification: higher levels as executable specs (slow/simple reference implementation). Lowering produces optimized code. Verify: ∀ inputs: fast_version(x) == slow_spec(x).

v2 example structure clarified: Dataflow = flat DAG with explicit wiring and shared nodes. AST = nested tree with duplicated references. Dataflow shows data dependencies, AST shows syntactic structure. Code generated FROM structured AST, not stored as string.
v2 full gradient experiment committed: calculator example with vision→architecture→component→function→dataflow→AST layers, READMEs for v1 and v2

Verification via mocking: tests live at function layer (last described layer). Lower layers (dataflow, AST) inherit tests through implemented_by edges. Higher layers are organizational, no executable tests. Tests ARE the intent, expressed as examples.
AST layer can be derived from dataflow - not hand-authored. Dataflow is complete enough: state→globals, switch→if-else, effect→call, op→op. The compiles_to edge becomes actual compilation.
Authoring boundary: human/AI writes Vision→Architecture→Component→Function→Dataflow. Tools derive AST from dataflow, WAT from AST. Humans describe intent down to dataflow, machines handle the rest.

Binaryen: WASM compiler infrastructure. Tree-based IR (like our AST), Relooper converts CFG→structured WASM, includes optimizer. Used by Emscripten, AssemblyScript. Could be v2+ backend for optimization, but can skip for now and generate WAT directly.
v2: examples (max, abs, calculator), dataflow→WAT compiler, protocol command
v2 WASM verification: vite test runner compiles dataflow→WAT→WASM, all tests pass
Extend dataflow→WAT compiler to support state (globals), effects (imports), and control flow (if/else, blocks) for calculator example

Calculator refactored to functional state-threading: on_key(acc,buf,op,key)→(new_acc,new_buf,new_op). Pure dataflow, no mutation, state changes explicit in edges. Compiler needs multi-value return support.
Multi-value return support added to dataflow→WAT compiler, calculator tests passing

Dataflow JSON is serialization, not authoring format. Visual whiteboard is the authoring interface - draw nodes, wire connections, see data flow. JSON verbosity irrelevant when you never write it by hand. Precedent: spreadsheets, Unreal Blueprints, Max/MSP, circuit schematics. Stack: Whiteboard (visual) → JSON (storage) → WAT (execution). Conversation layer assists wiring.
Dataflow visualization added to test runner with vis-network - nodes color-coded by kind, hierarchical LR layout
Context bloat concern: dataflow JSON is ~180 lines vs ~15 lines equivalent code. AI re-reads full graph every turn. Verbosity acceptable for visual whiteboard but terrible for LLM context windows.

Training mismatch: LLMs trained on billions of lines of code syntax (if/else, loops, functions). Very few dataflow graphs in training data. AI intuition for code patterns is deep - asking it to work in graphs may fight the training rather than leverage it. AI might perform WORSE on dataflow than on code.

Graph manipulation interface: instead of AI reading/writing full JSON, AI issues commands - add_node(), wire(), delete(). Tool maintains graph state, AI speaks in verbs not nouns. Solves context bloat (small commands vs full dump) and training mismatch ('wire X to Y' is natural language).

Alternative AI for graphs: LLMs are text predictors, dataflow is a graph. Better fits might be: Graph Neural Networks (native node/edge understanding), Program Synthesis (Sketch, Rosette - constraint-based from specs), SMT solvers (given tests, FIND the wiring), Neuro-symbolic (symbolic graph + neural intuition). Dataflow graph might BE the latent space that needs structure-native AI.
Design the ADR ↔ knowledge-graph ↔ test-surface relation so tests become a materialized spec
nodes.metadata_json: {"branch":"main","confidence":85,"prompt":"i have been thinking right now -> there are ADRs -> architectural decisions that are made -> there is a knowledge graph with these ADRs as a sort of tag, coming together of knowledge -> tests become the materialized spec -> how to make this clear relation between ADR, knowledge graph and test surface -> i have been playing around with TDD, but i often found to rely purely on an llm in an unstructured way leads to a lot of redundant and unfocused tests"}

nodes.title: Write HANDOFF.md capturing the ADR↔graph↔test thread for a fresh session

Hive (../hive, github.com/bigmistqke/hive) is already event-sourced: git commits are the event log, SQLite is the materialized view. 'Tests become the materialized spec' is that same architecture one level up — decisions are the log, tests are the view. Hive already has topics (-t), ADR status lifecycle (pending/active/completed/rejected), and contradicts/alternative_to edges.

Decisions should be COMPOSED, not unstructured text. A decision decomposes into claims/constraints; tests attach to the leaves. This is mycelium's own core move (node #289: code generated FROM structured AST, not stored as string) applied recursively to ADRs themselves. Kills the citation-edge idea: the test surface IS the leaf set of decomposed decisions, not a separate artifact linked by citations.

CORRECTION: the 29 'permanently pending' decisions are not metadata rot. 22 are v0 implementation decisions, executed then abandoned with v0; 2 are v1 scope (222 superseded by 264); 1 is v2 direction (done); 247 is still live. The status stayed pending because deciduous/hive have no RETIREMENT concept - no status means 'this was right, we did it, then its exploration was abandoned'.

Composition makes decision status DERIVED, not declared. Claims bottom out in tests, so: tests exist+pass = decision live; tests gone because constrained code is gone = decision auto-retired; new claims contradict old claims = superseded, with the exact colliding claim identified. Same trick as hive's materialized view and v2's derived AST: don't store it, derive it from the layer below. Solves metadata maintenance by eliminating the metadata.

Decision parts are TYPED (heterogeneous), not uniform. Only commitments bear tests; rationale/consequence are context. Mirrors v2 node #291 where higher layers are organizational and only the function layer bears tests - the decision contains its own copy of that boundary.

The pipeline is an HOURGLASS: observations (142, wide) → decision+propositions (30, narrow waist) → tests+code (wide). Unstructured LLM TDD fails because it goes prompt→tests directly, skipping the waist: wide→wide with no narrowing, so tests are unbounded and redundant. The waist is what BOUNDS the test surface. The 142:30 observation:decision ratio in the existing graph is the hourglass already showing itself.

v0's code knowledge graph is the substrate decisions TAG. 'ADRs as tags on the knowledge graph' is literal: a decision tags a region of the code graph. Gives orphan-code detection (code no decision explains) and makes retirement mode 3 computable (code region gone → decision retires). This is how v0 earns a place in v3.

EMPIRICAL: mutation-tested v2's max example (5 hand-written tests) through the real compiler+WASM. Only T1{3,5} and T5{0,-1} are load-bearing; T2{7,2} and T4{-3,-7} are redundant (subsumed by T5); T3{4,4} is VACUOUS (kills zero mutants - when a==b any impl returning either input passes). T1+T5 kills every mutant the full suite kills. 60% noise, and the noise is the plausible-looking part: T4 LOOKS like it covers negatives but passes under unsigned compare; only {0,-1} crosses zero and catches signedness. The user's original complaint, reproduced and measured on their own code.

Design nuance found by experiment: 'one test per leaf' != 'minimal suite'. Mutation says 2 tests suffice for max; the leaf decomposition says 3 (b>a→b, a>b→a, compare-is-signed) because one test can prove two leaves at once. Choose one-test-per-leaf deliberately: the goal was tests with a REASON, not the smallest suite. Mutation testing's job is checking whether a leaf split is REAL, not minimizing the suite. Caveat: equivalent mutants (ge_s == gt_s for max) are killed by nothing and that is correct, not a gap.

v3 is a HARNESS, not a data model. claude -p (headless) did not exist when mycelium was written; now the pipeline can be executed programmatically. The harness alternates LLM stages with DETERMINISTIC gates: propose propositions+guards (LLM) → gap/contradiction check (solver, no LLM) → human review (the waist) → one test per leaf (LLM, bounded) → mutation check for redundancy (no LLM) → implement (LLM) → tests run. This makes VISION.md's 'LLMs reason; tools verify' executable rather than aspirational.

The harness RESOLVES the v2 tension (#302-#305). #302 context bloat: each claude -p call gets only what it needs (one proposition → one test), never the full graph. #303 training mismatch: the LLM works in CODE and PREDICATES - what it is best at - never in graphs. The graph becomes the HARNESS's internal state, not the LLM's working medium. #304 verb interface: the harness IS the verb interface. The graph was never meant to be the AI's authoring surface; it is the orchestrator's bookkeeping.
Write packages/v3/DESIGN.md - the full design: hourglass, propositions with guards, three deterministic checks, derived status, harness stages, rendering layer

DESIGN.md written to packages/v3. Model: decisions compose into propositions (text/guard/answer/verified_by), recursive, one test per leaf. Three deterministic checks: gaps+contradictions over guards (solver), redundancy+vacuity over tests (mutation), status over graph (derived). Harness = LLM stages separated by non-LLM gates. Rendering layer = code-shaped text + fisheye + v0 descriptions. First build: run harness on clamp, print mutation score. Baseline to beat: hand-written max = 2/5 load-bearing (60% noise). Both experiment scripts preserved in packages/v3/experiments and verified runnable.

TEMPLATES: a template = (domain, guard language, completeness checker, redundancy checker). The architecture (3 checks, derived status, harness) is invariant; only what a guard QUANTIFIES OVER varies. Four: function (input space; SMT+mutation; demonstrated), structure (v0 code graph; v1's must_connect/must_not_connect - ALREADY BUILT), protocol (traces; property-based/model checking; not built, the hard one), bet (no domain; review/none). v1 is NOT roleless - its constraints.ts IS the structure template.

Refresh-token reuse is JWT's min>max. 'A refresh token can be used at most once' says the second use is not ALLOWED but not what HAPPENS - a gap, and the gap IS the replay attack. For functions an unspecified input is a bug; for protocols an unspecified TRACE is a vulnerability. The templates where guards are hardest to write are the ones where gaps are worth the most.

CORRECTION to #321: templates are SCALE, not taxonomy. A template is the guard language available at a given DEPTH. Decomposed far enough everything bottoms out in functions: JWT → 'refresh used at most once' (trace) → 'useRefreshToken(t) where t.used → error' (input guard) → test. No plugin system needed.

FRAME CONDITIONS: descending a scale is only sound if you emit the structural constraints that hold the composition together. revoke() sets revoked=true and validate() checks it - both green - but the invariant fails unless NOTHING ELSE writes revoked=false. That claim lives in no function. v0's side-effect tracking (reads/writes to shared state, scope crossings) IS the frame-condition checker. Corollary: unit tests without frame conditions are UNSOUND DECOMPOSITION - why suites of green unit tests still ship broken systems.

ONE LADDER: v2's gradient (vision→architecture→component→function→dataflow→AST) and v3's waist (decision→proposition→sub-proposition→leaf→test) are the SAME structure. One rule at every rung: a LEAF is verified by a test; a COMPOSITE is verified by its children being verified PLUS the frame conditions that make their composition sound. This is exactly #291 restated. Also reframes the test pyramid: verify a high proposition directly (property-based, expensive) or by decomposition+frame conditions (cheap, sound only if frames are checked).

ATTACK 3 REFUTED by ../solid-three. Claimed the design only fits crisp-semantics projects and not the user's UI/creative work. Wrong: 73 library fixes vs 42 site fixes, and the split is exactly the specifiable boundary. Library bugs map onto the templates: 'keep installEngine reachable only through initializePlugin' = must_not_connect (structure); 'assign ref before mounting children' = ordering invariant (protocol); 'release capture on unmount' = lifecycle invariant (protocol); 'default dpr to 1 for renderers without getPixelRatio' = a GUARD whose case was never specified = a GAP = clamp(5,10,3) in disguise. Site bugs (FOUC, sidebar, fonts, margins) are genuinely unspecifiable and the model correctly marks them verified_by:none. ERROR IN MY REASONING: confused the medium with the problem. solid-three is not a renderer (three.js is) - it is a RECONCILER, a seam. Seams are maximally specifiable.

solid-three is a hand-rolled implementation of the v3 design. Its test names ARE propositions: 'core owns no picking machinery', 'no engine no events', 'disjoint provenance: a click on one namespace mesh never reaches the other engine registry' (a FRAME CONDITION), 'two pointerEvents() instances install one manager and dispatch once'. And: 'warns and last-wins when two engines contribute the same canvas prop' IS clamp(5,10,3) - a contradiction found by hand and resolved by decision. And 'test(boundary): make token-stability test falsifiable' = the user caught a VACUOUS test (the T3 problem) by hand. THEREFORE: v3 does not introduce a methodology. It AUTOMATES WHAT THE USER ALREADY DOES BY HAND WHEN BEING CAREFUL.

EXPERIMENT: mutation-test solid-three's 252-test suite (built with Claude over months) to measure LLM-induced test redundancy. Working on a COPY (user's tree was dirty with uncommitted events work - never mutate a dirty repo). 60 mutants across 15 core modules, ~50s per full-suite run. Smoke test already telling: props.ts:42 ===→!== killed by 145 of 248 tests (mass redundancy signal); create-three.tsx:92 ??→|| SURVIVED (coverage gap).

verified_by gains a fourth mode: TYPE. 'A guard is a type the language cannot express.' clamp(i32,i32,i32) is a LIE - the real signature is 'where min <= max'. The guard is the RESIDUE: the part of the contract the type system could not hold (= refinement types, already in PRIOR_ART). Ordering is strict, not peer: type proves the claim for ALL inputs at ALL call sites statically; test proves it only for the inputs you thought of. RULE: lift into the type system whatever you can, guard only the residue.

Every gap now has THREE resolutions, not two: HANDLE it (define behaviour → verified_by:test), PROMISE it (precondition, hope → verified_by:none), or MAKE IT UNREPRESENTABLE (a Range type constructible only when valid → verified_by:type). The third deletes the gap rather than filling it. solid-three does this by instinct: 'fix(types): make the plugins prop real, stop loose plugins swallowing every prop' IS a proposition promoted from test to type. HONEST COST: lifting into types buys correctness with ergonomic friction (a Range type makes clamp annoying to call). The harness must SUGGEST the lift and name its cost, never demand it.
v3 design committed: DESIGN.md + the two experiments that back it (mutate.ts, exhaustive.ts). HANDOFF.md kept but marked superseded.

BLIND TEST PASSED. Cold claude -p, one prompt, one file (hive event-store.ts), no session context → 29 propositions, 14 gaps, 8 contradictions. Beat my own careful pass: found 7 of my 8 findings plus several I missed, often sharper. One CONFIRMED by test (a confidence transition is re-materialized as a STATUS on rebuild - node status literally becomes '95'). The design's top open risk - can an LLM produce propositions with teeth - is RETIRED. Answer: yes.

The VERIFY GATE earned its place empirically. 22 claims in → 1 test-confirmed, 1 code-traced, 20 unverified. And 2 of my own 3 probes were INVALID (passed while testing nothing). Without a non-LLM gate we would have shipped 22 'findings', most unproven. 'LLMs reason; tools verify' is no longer a principle - it is a measured result.

DELETE the rendering layer from the design. Fisheye views, code-shaped serialization, cached descriptions - all designed to solve context bloat (#302). Unnecessary: the cold agent was handed ONE file and went and read add.ts, status.ts, custom-db.ts, nodes.ts on its own. You do not convey the graph to the model; you give it an ENTRY POINT and let it fetch. #302/#303 are not solved by clever rendering - they are solved by not doing it.

NEW blind-spot category the design lacks: TEST-DOUBLE DIVERGENCE. hive's 162-test suite is green and structurally CANNOT reach the incremental replay path - the test context's db is in-memory so dbExists is permanently false. Not vacuity (a test that cannot fail), not a coverage gap - the test HARNESS silently disables a production code path. The fixtures are part of the specified system. A frame condition on the test double, not the code.

Blind test recorded and committed (9afcfce): prompt, raw cold-pass output, sealed hand pass, probe tests, README. Rendering layer deleted from DESIGN.md. Open question 6 added (test-double divergence). 'What to build first' superseded: clamp is moot - build the VERIFY GATE.

CORRECTION to #334. 'Let the agent fetch' was too broad. The blind test proved the model can fetch CODE (structural handles: imports, call sites, self-guiding). It did NOT prove it can fetch INTENT - event-store.ts had no intent to fetch, so the cold pass RECONSTRUCTED mechanism from source, which is precisely the inverse problem VISION.md exists to abolish. THE ASYMMETRY: code is PRESENT in the repo so the agent can fetch it; intent is ABSENT so it must be supplied. You cannot grep for the decision you do not know exists.

EVIDENCE for the correction, from the experiment itself: the cold pass produced 22 gaps and could NOT RANK ONE. It could not tell a violated commitment from a deliberate deferral (pulse's commit() dropping cleanups; hive's unread conflict refs; write-only status fields) because it had NO DECISIONS to compare against. That is why 22 claims needed a human to sort and only 1 survived. Intent is not decoration - it is what makes findings RANKABLE. A model with the decisions could have sorted most of that list itself.

The graph's job is NOT to be rendered into context. It is to be INDEXED BY CODE LOCATION, so the agent can ask 'what was decided about this file?'. That is the 'decisions tag regions of the code graph' edge (the v0 tie-in) - and it is the HANDLE that makes intent fetchable at all. Code retrieval is self-guiding (an import tells you what to read next); decision retrieval has no handles until we build this one. Build the edge, and intent retrieval becomes self-guiding the way code retrieval already is.

DESIGN.md and blind-test README corrected; committed c4048d9. The deletion stands for CODE (agent fetches, self-guiding) and is REVERSED for INTENT in a smaller shape: not a rendering layer, ONE EDGE from a region of code to the decisions that constrain it.

ENCODE THE GRAPH INTO COMMIT MESSAGES (git trailers). The missing code→intent edge already exists in every repo: git blame. line → blame → commit → trailer 'Decision: 247' → node → reasoning. This makes intent retrieval SELF-GUIDING by the same mechanism as code retrieval: an import says what to read next; a blame says what to read next. No MCP server, no index, no rendering layer. This is node #270 ('introspection like git blame but for intent') - the metaphor IS the implementation.

The commit-trailer edge beats deciduous's --commit HEAD on four counts: (1) DIRECTION - stores commit→node, which is the way retrieval needs to go, not node→commit; (2) LOCATION - lives in git history, so it survives the tool dying; (3) DISTRIBUTION - travels with git push, no patch files; (4) REVERSE LOOKUP - 'git log --grep' gives every commit implementing a decision, which is node #271 (reverse introspection) for free. Also: commit messages are IMMUTABLE and decisions get superseded - that is correct, not a bug. The commit records what was decided THEN; the graph records what is true NOW. Commit messages are the log, the graph is the view - hive's architecture one level down.

RISKS of commit-trailer encoding: (1) reformatting destroys blame - standard problem, standard fix (.git-blame-ignore-revs); (2) squash concatenates messages so trailers survive, rebase preserves them - robust enough; (3) granularity - one commit may carry 3 decision refs, but that narrows 340 nodes to 3; (4) THE REAL ONE - people forget. Same metadata rot as everything else. BUT it is the cheapest version of that risk: you are writing the commit anyway, and it is the ONLY mechanism in the design enforceable by a commit-msg hook.
Build the trace loop: commit-msg hook enforcing a Decision: <uuid> trailer with file-overlap verification, plus a blame command walking file:line → commit → trailer → node

Trace loop SHIPPED and closes in both directions. commit-msg hook: rejects no-trailer, rejects nonexistent node, rejects real-node-with-wrong-files (the confabulation guard), accepts honest citation. 'trace why file:line' walks blame→commit→trailer→node; 'trace code <id>' walks the reverse (node #271, specced in January, now built). Baseline measured: 102 commits, 0 citing a decision, 0% traceable. The hook found a bug in ITSELF during testing - a trailing slash in a declared path caused a FALSE REJECTION of an honest citation, which is the dangerous failure mode for a gate (teaches people to use --no-verify). Fixed.
Export the decision graph to docs/ for the web viewer
